topics.title: Revision of jss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the functions of an office.
The students should be able to list different types of business documents.
The students should be able to explain the basic concept of book keeping.
Introduction:
Last term we studied about commerce and office management. Today we will revise what we learned in JSS 2 to prepare for this term's new topics.
Content:
We will review the key points from last term. An office is the center of business activities where records are kept and decisions are made. Business documents like receipts and invoices are important for recording transactions. Book keeping involves recording financial transactions in a systematic way. We will use examples like market stalls in Onitsha to show how these concepts apply in real life Nigerian businesses.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create a simple business scenario and identify which documents would be needed for transactions.
Evaluation questions:
1. What are the main functions of an office?
2. List three types of business documents.
3. Why is book keeping important for a business?
4. How does book keeping help a market trader like Alhaji at Balogun Market?
Summary:
Today we reviewed the fundamentals of office management and book keeping which form the foundation for this term's Business Studies topics.

topics.title: The office
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the functions of an office.
The students should be able to differentiate between different office layouts.
The students should be able to explain how office layout affects productivity.
Introduction:
Last week we reviewed JSS 2 work including the concept of an office. Today we will study the office in more detail, focusing on its functions and how it should be arranged.
Content:
An office has many important functions including record keeping, communication, planning and decision making. Common office layouts include open plan, private offices and cubicles. An open plan layout like in many Nigerian banks allows for easy communication but may have noise issues. A private office layout provides privacy but may limit teamwork. The layout should consider factors like workflow, space available and the type of work done. For example, a law firm in Lagos might need private offices for client meetings while a newspaper office might prefer open plan for collaboration.
Class activity:
Students will draw their ideal office layout for a school business club and explain why they arranged it that way.
Evaluation questions:
1. List three functions of an office.
2. What is the difference between open plan and private office layouts?
3. How would you arrange an office for a company selling goods at Alaba International Market?
4. Why is good office layout important?
Summary:
Understanding office functions and proper layout helps businesses operate efficiently and create a productive work environment.

topics.title: Office equipment
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of office equipment.
The students should be able to explain the uses of common office machines.
The students should be able to state the rules for caring for office equipment.
Introduction:
We have studied about the office and its functions. Today we will learn about the equipment used in offices, how they work and how to take care of them.
Content:
Common office equipment includes computers, printers, photocopiers, scanners and calculators. A computer is used for typing documents, storing information and communicating. A printer produces paper copies of documents. In Nigerian businesses like banks, these machines are used daily to serve customers. Proper care of equipment includes keeping them clean, covering them when not in use, and using them correctly. For example, in a busy office in Port Harcourt, printers need regular maintenance to avoid paper jams. Equipment should be placed in a well-ventilated area away from direct sunlight or rain which can damage them.
Class activity:
Students will identify office equipment in the school and create a poster showing how to properly care for each item.
Evaluation questions:
1. Name three types of office equipment.
2. What is the purpose of a photocopier?
3. Explain how to properly care for a computer in an office.
4. Why is it important to maintain office equipment regularly?
Summary:
Office equipment helps work get done efficiently, and proper care ensures they last longer and work better.

topics.title: Business documents
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of business documents.
The students should be able to explain the purpose of each document.
The students should be able to fill in business documents correctly.
Introduction:
In our previous lessons, we have learned about offices and equipment. Today we will study business documents which are important for recording business transactions.
Content:
Business documents are written records of business activities. Common types include invoices, receipts, orders and letters. An invoice is a bill sent to a customer showing goods or services provided and the amount owed. A receipt is proof that payment has been received. An order is a document requesting goods or services. For example, when you buy gala at a bus stop, you get a receipt. When a company in Kano buys goods from a supplier, they get an invoice. Each document has specific information that must be included like dates, names, amounts and descriptions. Students must learn to fill these documents accurately to avoid mistakes in business.
Class activity:
Students will practice filling out sample invoices and receipts for a fictional school canteen transaction.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the purpose of an invoice?
2. List three types of business documents.
3. What information must be included on a receipt?
4. How would you fill out an order form for buying textbooks from a publisher?
Summary:
Business documents are essential for recording transactions and maintaining proper records in any business operation.

topics.title: Book keeping: double entry
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the concept of double entry book keeping.
The students should be able to identify debit and credit entries.
The students should be able to post entries to ledger accounts.
Introduction:
We have studied business documents which record transactions. Today we will learn how these transactions are recorded in a systematic way using double entry book keeping.
Content:
Double entry book keeping is a system where every transaction affects at least two accounts. Each transaction has a debit entry and a credit entry. Debit entries increase asset and expense accounts, while credit entries increase liability and income accounts. For example, when a business in Lagos sells goods for N10,000 cash, the cash account is debited N10,000 and the sales account is credited N10,000. This system helps ensure accuracy because total debits must equal total credits. We will practice posting entries to different ledger accounts like cash, sales, purchases and expenses.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to record sample transactions using the double entry system in simple ledger accounts.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is double entry book keeping?
2. What is the difference between debit and credit entries?
3. How would you record the sale of goods for cash in a market?
4. Why is it important that total debits equal total credits?
Summary:
Double entry book keeping is a systematic method of recording transactions that helps maintain accurate financial records.

topics.title: Trial balance
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to prepare a trial balance.
The students should be able to identify common errors in book keeping.
The students should be able to explain the purpose of a trial balance.
Introduction:
Last week we learned about double entry book keeping where every transaction has equal debit and credit entries. Today we will learn how to check if our entries are balanced using a trial balance.
Content:
A trial balance is a statement that lists all accounts with their debit and credit balances to check if they are equal. It is prepared at the end of an accounting period. If total debits equal total credits, it means our double entries are probably correct. Common errors that can cause imbalance include posting to the wrong side, wrong amounts, or missing entries. For example, a small business in Abuja might have recorded a N5,000 expense as N500, which would make the trial balance unbalanced. When errors are found, they must be corrected before preparing financial statements.
Class activity:
Students will be given a set of ledger accounts and will prepare a trial balance, then identify and correct any errors.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is a trial balance?
2. What does it mean if total debits equal total credits in a trial balance?
3. Name two common errors that can make a trial balance unbalanced.
4. How would you correct an error where you posted N2,000 to the wrong account?
Summary:
A trial balance is an important tool to check the accuracy of book keeping before preparing final accounts.

topics.title: Trading account
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the purpose of a trading account.
The students should be able to calculate gross profit.
The students should be able to prepare a simple trading account.
Introduction:
We have learned about book keeping and trial balance. Today we will study the trading account, which is used to calculate the profit from buying and selling goods.
Content:
A trading account shows the results of buying and selling goods during a period. It calculates gross profit, which is the difference between sales revenue and cost of goods sold. Cost of goods sold includes opening stock, purchases and direct expenses, minus closing stock. For example, a shop in Onitsha that sells yams might have opening stock of N10,000, purchases of N20,000, and closing stock of N8,000. The cost of goods sold would be N22,000. If sales were N35,000, the gross profit would be N13,000. The trading account helps businesses understand how profitable their main activities are.
Class activity:
Students will prepare a trading account for a fictional local business like a pepper seller in the market.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the purpose of a trading account?
2. How is gross profit calculated?
3. What items are included in cost of goods sold?
4. If a business has sales of N50,000, purchases of N30,000 and opening stock of N10,000, what is the gross profit?
Summary:
The trading account shows how profitable a business is in its main trading activities by calculating gross profit.

topics.title: Profit and loss account
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the purpose of a profit and loss account.
The students should be able to calculate net profit.
The students should be able to prepare a simple profit and loss account.
Introduction:
We studied the trading account which shows gross profit from trading activities. Today we will learn about the profit and loss account which shows the overall profitability of the business after all expenses.
Content:
A profit and loss account shows all incomes and expenses of a business to calculate net profit. It starts with gross profit from the trading account, then adds other incomes like interest received, and subtracts all expenses like rent, salaries, and electricity. For example, a small restaurant in Lagos might have gross profit of N100,000, but after deducting N20,000 for rent, N30,000 for salaries, and N10,000 for other expenses, the net profit would be N40,000. This account helps business owners understand if they are making money after paying all costs. Expenses are categorized as operating expenses like utilities, or administrative expenses like office supplies.
Class activity:
Students will prepare a profit and loss account for a fictional business like a recharge card seller, using given figures.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between gross profit and net profit?
2. List three types of business expenses.
3. How would you calculate net profit in a profit and loss account?
4. Why is a profit and loss account important for a business owner?
Summary:
The profit and loss account shows the overall profitability of a business by deducting all expenses from gross profit to get net profit.

topics.title: Balance sheet basics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify assets and liabilities.
The students should be able to explain the accounting equation.
The students should be able to prepare a simple balance sheet.
Introduction:
We have studied accounts that show business performance. Today we will learn about the balance sheet, which shows the financial position of a business at a specific time.
Content:
A balance sheet shows what a business owns (assets) and what it owes (liabilities) at a particular date. Assets are resources owned by the business like cash, equipment, and buildings. Liabilities are amounts owed to others like loans and supplier credit. The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. For example, a small shop in Kano might have assets worth N500,000 including N100,000 cash and N400,000 worth of goods. If it has liabilities of N200,000 to suppliers, the owner's equity would be N300,000. The balance sheet must always balance because what the business owns must equal what it owes plus what the owner has invested.
Class activity:
Students will create a simple balance sheet for a fictional business like a small provision store in their community.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between assets and liabilities?
2. What is the accounting equation?
3. List three examples of business assets.
4. If a business has assets of N200,000 and liabilities of N50,000, what is the owner's equity?
Summary:
The balance sheet shows the financial position of a business by listing its assets and liabilities, which must always be equal.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall key concepts from the term.
The students should be able to solve past BECE questions.
The students should be able to identify areas needing more study.
Introduction:
This is our last week of the term. We will revise all the topics we have studied and practice questions similar to what you will see in your BECE exam.
Content:
We will review the main topics from this term including office functions, equipment, business documents, double entry book keeping, trial balance, trading account, profit and loss account, and balance sheet. Students will work through past BECE Business Studies questions, learning to read carefully and select the best answers. We will discuss common mistakes and how to avoid them. For example, in book keeping questions, students often confuse debit and credit entries. In financial statement questions, they might forget to include all items. We will practice time management to ensure you can complete all questions in the exam.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create revision flashcards for key terms and concepts, then test each other.
Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the difference between gross profit and net profit.
2. What is the purpose of a trial balance?
3. List three functions of an office.
4. How would you record a cash sale in double entry book keeping?
5. Why is it important to maintain proper business documents?
Summary:
Today we reviewed all the key topics from this term and practiced exam questions to prepare for your BECE Business Studies examination.
